title: The Duty of Memory
author: Study The Great Books
summary: The founder of Study The Great Books reaches back to Plato's Phaedrus, in which the Egyptian god Thamus warns that writing will produce forgetfulness rather than wisdom because people will trust external marks instead of their own memory, to argue that the same warning applies with far greater force to ChatGPT, Google, and Gemini today. Despite founding a publication devoted to reading books, the author concedes Socrates' central point: external repositories of knowledge, whether ancient scrolls or a smartphone, become "the enemy of human good" whenever they let a person collect information without ever internalizing it, leaving them, in Socrates' words, with "the show of wisdom without the reality." The piece grounds this in a specifically Christian argument about the purpose of knowledge, that man's good lies in the attainment of virtue as an image-bearer of God, and that knowledge is a necessary link in the chain from wisdom to prudence to right action, meaning knowledge stored only externally cannot do the moral work God calls people to. It closes with a concrete call to intentional memorization, of scripture, poetry, or basic facts, framed not as a nostalgic exercise but as a duty tied to reclaiming a capacity for genuine understanding that ubiquitous lookup tools have allowed people to atrophy.
points: The Phaedrus citation is used with real precision, not just as classical decoration: Thamus's specific warning that writing will produce 'hearers of many things' who 'have learned nothing' and possess 'the show of wisdom without the reality' is applied directly to how people relate to AI chatbots today.

The author performs a notable self-aware move, explicitly conceding that Socrates' anti-writing argument threatens his own vocation as a books-publication founder, then affirming it anyway: 'if one relies on them to carry knowledge so that we don't have to then books become the enemy of human good.'

The piece builds a specific theological chain of reasoning (knowledge is a prerequisite for wisdom, wisdom for prudence, prudence for right action) to argue that knowledge stored only externally cannot do the moral work of virtue formation, not merely that memorization is a nice academic habit.

The closing practical instruction is concrete rather than aspirational: readers are told to commit specific categories of content, scripture, poetry, multiplication tables, geography, to memory as a discipline, tying the essay's classical/theological argument to an actionable habit rather than leaving it purely diagnostic.
quotes: This discovery of yours will create forgetfulness in the learners' souls, because they will not use their memories; they will trust to the external written characters and not remember of themselves.

The specific which you have discovered is an aid not to memory, but to reminiscence, and you give your disciples not truth, but only the semblance of truth; they will be hearers of many things and will have learned nothing; they will appear to be omniscient and will generally know nothing; they will be tiresome company, having the show of wisdom without the reality.

The person with a vast library, in one sense, has much knowledge available to him, but he does not himself know anything unless he takes it upon himself to inscribe that knowledge not only in books but on his own soul.

What your average person knows today often doesn't rival what a sixth grader knew in the 1940's. We rely on something else, something external, to contain the knowledge for us and we are content to look it up only if and when it becomes relevant and, in most cases, we release that information back into the void about 15 seconds later.

Knowledge is a prerequisite for wisdom and wisdom is a prerequisite for prudence and prudence is knowing what is right and true, understanding what one ought to do in light of that knowledge, and then actually doing it when the time for action comes.

Socrates' point is well made because the fool of his day would treat books like the fool of our day treats ChatGPT, an excuse not to know, not to be made better by effort and intentional engagement in learning.
